table.caption: Jars of honey a farm offers each week at four prices (invented data for practice)

supply-s2.title: A year in the smartphone market
supply-s2.text: In one year in the market for smartphones in Lindmoor, an invented country: (1) the price of the computer chips used in every phone falls by a third; (2) three new phone makers open factories; (3) the government puts a new tax of \$20 on every phone a maker sells; (4) a popular video makes buyers want the newest phones more than ever.

items.q: The price of flour rises. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for bread.

why.correct: Higher input costs make each loaf costlier to make, so bakers offer fewer loaves at every price: supply shifts left.

key.because: a rise in the price of flour, an input

slips.D: Flour is an input for bakers, so its price shifts supply; buyers' wants have not changed.

items.q: A new machine lets furniture makers build chairs faster and more cheaply. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for chairs.

why.correct: Better technology lowers the cost of each chair, so makers offer more at every price: supply shifts right.

key.because: a technology that lowers the cost of making chairs

slips.D: The machine changes what makers can offer, so it shifts supply, not demand.

items.q: The government pays solar panel makers a subsidy for each panel they produce. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for solar panels.

why.correct: A subsidy lowers producers' cost per unit, so they offer more at every price: supply shifts right.

key.because: a subsidy paid to producers for each panel

slips.D: The subsidy goes to producers, so it shifts supply.

items.q: The government starts collecting a tax from producers on every bottle of soda sold. Shift the right curve the right way in the market for soda.

why.correct: A per-unit tax on producers works like a higher cost, so they offer less at every price: supply shifts left.

key.because: a tax collected from producers on each bottle

slips.D: The tax is paid by producers, so it shifts supply.

items.q: The market price of honey rises and nothing else changes. Place point X where the farm ends up on its supply curve.

why.correct: A higher price moves sellers up along the supply curve to a larger quantity supplied. The curve does not shift.

items.q: Using the table, by how many jars a week does the quantity supplied rise when the price rises from \$6 to \$10?

why.correct: At \$6 the farm offers 40 jars and at \$10 it offers 80: $80 - 40 = 40$ more jars.

mistakes.why: That is the change in price. The question asks for the change in the quantity supplied: 80 - 40.
You added the quantities. The change is the difference: 80 - 40.

options: An increase in supply as the price rises
The law of supply: a higher price brings a larger quantity supplied
An inverse relationship between price and quantity supplied
A shift of the supply curve to the right each time the price changes

why.correct: Each \$2 rise in price brings 20 more jars offered, along one supply curve: the law of supply.
options: A price change moves along the supply curve; supply itself does not change.
Right: price and quantity supplied rise together.
Both rise together: a direct relationship.
The table is one supply curve; only the price changes.

items.q: A drought raises the farm's costs, and it now offers 10 fewer jars at every price in the table. What happened?
options: Supply decreased: the supply curve shifted left
Quantity supplied fell along the same supply curve
Supply increased, because honey became scarcer
Demand for honey decreased

why.correct: Fewer jars offered at every price, because of higher costs, is a decrease in supply: a shift left.
options: Right: a cost increase shifts supply left.
A movement along the curve needs a change in the honey price.
Offering less at every price is a decrease in supply.
The drought changed the farm's costs, not what buyers want.

items.q: Honey makers expect the price of honey to rise sharply next month. What happens to the supply of honey this month?
options: It increases, because makers rush to produce more honey
The quantity supplied rises along the curve this month
It is unchanged until the price actually rises
It decreases, because makers hold back jars to sell later at the higher price

why.correct: Expectations are a determinant of supply. Expecting a higher price later, sellers offer less now: today's supply shifts left.
options: Producing more takes time; the jars on hand are held back for the higher price.
Today's price has not changed, so there is no movement along the curve.
Expectations shift supply before the price changes.
Right: sellers store jars for next month.

items.q: Event (1): the price of chips falls by a third. What happens in the smartphone market?
options: Supply decreases, because the chip makers now earn less per chip
Demand increases, because phones get cheaper to buy
Supply increases, because each phone costs less to make
Quantity supplied falls along the supply curve

why.correct: Chips are an input. Lower input costs mean makers offer more phones at every price: supply shifts right.
options: The question is about phone makers, whose costs fell.
The chip price changes phone makers' costs, not what buyers want at each price.
Right: lower input costs shift supply right.
The phone price did not change, so this is a shift, not a movement.

items.q: Event (2): three new phone makers open factories. What happens to the market supply of phones?
options: It decreases, because existing makers lose customers
It increases, because there are more sellers
It stays the same, because demand did not change
Quantity supplied rises along the curve

why.correct: The number of sellers is a determinant of supply: more sellers shift market supply right.
options: Existing makers may sell less, but the market as a whole offers more.
Right: more sellers offer more phones at every price.
Supply can shift without any change in demand.
No price change is described, so the curve itself shifts.

items.q: Event (3): a tax of \$20 is collected from makers on every phone sold. What happens to the supply of phones?
options: It decreases: the supply curve shifts left
It increases: the supply curve shifts right
The quantity supplied rises along the curve
It is unchanged, because buyers pay the price

why.correct: A per-unit tax on sellers raises their cost of each phone, so they offer fewer at every price.
options: Right: a tax on producers works like a higher cost.
A subsidy would shift supply right; a tax shifts it left.
The tax changes costs, which shifts the curve rather than moving along it.
The tax is collected from makers, so their offers change.

items.q: Event (4): a popular video makes buyers want new phones more. Which curve does this event shift?
options: The supply curve, to the right
The supply curve, to the left
Neither curve; it is a movement along supply
The demand curve, to the right

why.correct: Tastes are a determinant of demand, not supply. The video shifts demand right; the supply curve stays put.
options: Makers' costs and numbers have not changed, so supply stays put.
Nothing here reduces what makers can offer at each price.
A change in tastes shifts a curve; it is the demand curve that moves.
Right: buyers' tastes shift demand.

items.q: Why does the supply curve slope upward?
options: Buyers want more at higher prices
Sellers' costs fall as the price rises
A higher price makes it worthwhile for sellers to produce more, even as extra output gets costlier
A higher price attracts more buyers

why.correct: Producing more usually costs more per extra unit, and a higher price covers those costs and makes the extra output profitable, so quantity supplied rises with price.
options: Buyers want less at higher prices; supply describes sellers.
Sellers' costs do not fall because the price rose.
Right: a higher price covers the cost of extra output.
Buyers are part of demand, not supply.

items.q: A reporter writes, "The price of gasoline rose, so the supply of gasoline increased." How should the sentence be fixed?
options: "The supply of gasoline decreased"; higher prices lower supply
"The quantity supplied of gasoline increased"; supply itself did not change
"The demand for gasoline increased"; price affects buyers
"Supply and quantity supplied both increased"

why.correct: A change in the good's own price changes the quantity supplied (a movement along the supply curve). "Supply" means the whole curve.
options: A higher price raises the quantity supplied; it does not lower supply.
Right: a price change is a movement along the curve.
The sentence is about sellers, and buyers want less at a higher price.
Only the quantity supplied changes; the curve stays put.

items.q: Make the explanation specific: the price of flour rises. Fill in each blank to explain what happens in the market for bread.

why.correct: Name the input, the effect on cost, and the direction of the shift.

specific.frame: Flour is ___ for bakers, so its higher price ___ their cost of each loaf, and the supply of bread shifts ___.

because.label: What flour is
options: an input
a substitute

why.1: Bakers use flour to make bread; it is an input, not something buyers choose instead of bread.

change.label: Bakers' cost
options: raises
lowers

why.1: A dearer input makes each loaf cost more to make.

direction.label: Which way supply shifts
options: left
right

why.1: Higher costs mean fewer loaves offered at every price, a shift left.

specific.model: Flour is an input for bakers, so a higher flour price raises the cost of making each loaf, and as a result bakers offer fewer loaves at every price: the supply of bread decreases and shifts left.
